Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: ExxonMobil has strong recent momentum (shares up about 57% in a year) and capable management, but it is a mature commodity producer, not a top dog in an emerging industry, and it lacks the brand-led, hard-to-copy advantage Gardner seeks. It fits few of the Rule Breaker traits.
summaries.buffett: Buffett values simple, durable businesses with predictable earnings; ExxonMobil is understandable and has world-class assets, but its earnings swing with oil prices (a $22,440M loss in 2020, $55,740M profit in 2022). Returns on capital of about 10% are adequate rather than exceptional, and at about 22 times trailing earnings there is no clear margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire ExxonMobil's discipline and low-cost Guyana and Permian barrels, but would note it sells a commodity at prices it cannot control. Inverting, the main risks are a collapse in oil prices, long-term demand decline and climate policy, which are real for any oil major.
summaries.lynch: ExxonMobil is a cyclical in Lynch's categories, and he warned that cyclicals look cheapest at peak earnings: its forward P/E of about 13 rests on oil prices lifted by the 2026 Hormuz disruption. The company keeps shrinking its share count, but insiders have not been buying.
summaries.fisher: ExxonMobil scores on Fisher's points for research depth, cost control and long-term planning, but it sells undifferentiated products with no special selling edge and modest margins (operating margin about 11%). Its growth depends more on commodity prices than on new products.
summaries.graham: ExxonMobil passes Graham's tests for size and dividend record (paid for more than a century, raised for over 40 years in a row), and EPS rose from $3.85 (2015) to $6.70 (2025). It fails on earnings stability (a 2020 loss) and on price: about 22 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B of about 62.
summaries.thiel: ExxonMobil does not fit Thiel's monopoly-through-technology view: it competes with many similar majors and national oil companies in a commodity market. Its Guyana position is a valuable cornered resource, but it is not a proprietary 10x technology.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's style favours secular growth compounders with clear catalysts; ExxonMobil's 2026 gains came from an oil-price spike and its long-term revenue growth is flat to slightly down. It could suit a tactical energy view but not his core long-duration growth approach.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades macro themes and price momentum, and ExxonMobil has both in 2026: Middle East supply disruption pushed oil up and the shares rose about 57% in a year. The thesis depends on oil staying high, which futures markets doubt, so it fits as a macro trade rather than a long-term holding.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-heavy businesses with modest returns and no pricing power, and ExxonMobil's ROIC of about 10% and gross margin near 30% fall short of his bar. It would not qualify as a 'good company' under his rules.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula ExxonMobil is middling: return on capital is around 10% and EV/EBIT of about 18.6 gives an earnings yield near 5.4%. Neither measure would rank it near the top.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, great management and great reinvestment; ExxonMobil has strong management and reinvests heavily in Guyana, the Permian and LNG, but its commodity business earns modest returns on that capital. It fits one or two legs rather than all three.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai buys simple businesses during temporary distress at deep discounts; ExxonMobil was such a case in 2020, but today it trades near record highs after the 2026 oil spike. Downside protection is decent thanks to low debt and low-cost assets, but the price is not a bargain.
summaries.wood: ExxonMobil is the opposite of ARK's disruptive-innovation focus; ARK sees electric vehicles and batteries reducing oil demand. Its lithium, carbon-capture and synthetic graphite projects are small relative to the oil and gas business.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with pricing power; ExxonMobil generates large cash flows (about $30.6B TTM free cash flow) but has no pricing power and unpredictable earnings. It does not fit his core criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model does not apply well to a commodity producer whose prices are set by the market. ExxonMobil's scale lowers its costs, but that benefit is kept as margin rather than passed to customers to build loyalty.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought large, fast-growing markets and products solving painful problems; ExxonMobil supplies essential energy but in a mature, slow-growing market. It is far from the kind of early-stage opportunity Sequoia looks for.
summaries.nash: ExxonMobil fails Tom Nash's process early: it is a commodity producer, one of his zones to avoid, debt ($42,368M) exceeds cash ($10,588M) and its trailing operating margin of 11.2% is below his 20% floor. Revenue has jumped in 2026 on an oil-price spike (up 44.1% in Q2), but it fell in 2023 and 2025, and its 13-category scorecard is about 65. The price implies about 20% annual revenue growth and his DCF gives roughly $56 a share against $174, so it fails his valuation steps too.

momentum.evidence: XOM rose about 57.2% in the 52 weeks to October 13, 2026 ($174.08), far ahead of the S&P 500 (SPY total return about 20.4%), after an all-time high of $176.41 on March 30, 2026.

g4.evidence: CEO Darren Woods is a respected operator, but the stock is held mainly by index funds rather than famous concentrated investors.

g6.evidence: After the 2026 rally some commentators call XOM fully valued, pointing to a 2026 consensus that assumes elevated oil prices, though its forward P/E of about 13 is not seen as extreme.

simple.evidence: ExxonMobil finds and produces oil and gas, refines it into fuels and makes chemicals, a business a careful generalist can follow.

b2.evidence: Results swing with commodity prices: a $22,440M loss in 2020, $55,740M net income in 2022 and $28,844M in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management reports candidly and has cut structural costs by $15.1B since 2019, but it has faced climate-disclosure litigation and shareholder fights such as Engine No. 1's 2021 board challenge.

b6.evidence: Acquisitions like Pioneer (2024) and Denbury (2023) fit its core strategy, though a $60B-scale deal also reflects the industry's consolidation race.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 10% and ROE about 12.6% with low debt ($42,368M against a $716B market value), decent but not high and not consistent across the cycle.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow was $23,612M on net income of $28,844M (about 82%), and TTM free cash flow was $30,553M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded Guyana and Permian growth, but the share price spent much of 2014-2020 falling, so retained profits did not always add matching value.

safety.evidence: Near record highs and at about 22 times trailing earnings, the price does not offer a margin of safety against a fall in oil prices.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 13 looks reasonable, but it rests on 2026 oil prices that futures markets expect to ease.

mu5.evidence: Low debt and low-cost assets make bankruptcy unlikely, but oil price collapses, energy transition and climate policy are several plausible ways to lose value.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in Guyana (fifth FPSO due 4Q26), the Permian and LNG at good returns, but returns depend on oil prices and resources deplete.

ly2.evidence: ExxonMobil is a classic cyclical whose story is volume growth from low-cost Guyana and Permian barrels plus cost cuts.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 22 is well above its long-run earnings growth; EPS fell from $8.89 in 2023 to $6.70 in 2025 before the 2026 spike.

runway.evidence: Revenue (total revenues and other income) was $332,238M in 2025, below 2022's $413,680M, and long-term oil demand growth is slow.

ly7.evidence: The share count fell about 3.9% in a year through buybacks, but the only insider trades in the last 12 months were sales (about $2.4M by a vice president).

ly8.evidence: XOM is one of the largest, most widely followed US stocks.

fi2.evidence: It is developing Proxxima resins, synthetic graphite, lithium and carbon capture, but these are small next to fuels and chemicals.

fi3.evidence: Research has produced process and catalyst gains and deepwater execution know-how, but new products add little to revenue so far.

fi4.evidence: Fuels and chemicals are sold largely on price, so selling skill is not a distinctive advantage.

longterm.evidence: Management invests through the cycle in multi-decade projects such as Guyana and LNG rather than managing for the next quarter.

gr1.evidence: ExxonMobil has a market value of about $716B and 2025 revenues of $332,238M.

ni10.evidence: It reported a net loss of $22,440M in 2020.

gr4.evidence: ExxonMobil has paid dividends for more than a century and has raised them for over 40 consecutive years; the current annual rate is $4.12 a share.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $3.85 in 2015 to $6.70 in 2025, up about 74%.

gr6.evidence: The price of $174.08 is about 22 times average EPS for 2023-2025 ($8.89, $7.84, $6.70).

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 22.4 times a P/B of about 2.76 gives about 62, above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its technology is strong but not ten times better than Chevron's, Shell's or Aramco's.

timing.evidence: 2026 Middle East supply disruption lifted oil prices, but long-term timing for oil demand is unfavourable as electrification grows.

th3.evidence: ExxonMobil is a century-old incumbent in a huge, mature market, not a company that started by dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: Darren Woods' team is a seasoned operator that delivered Guyana and the Pioneer deal, but it is not an exceptional founder team.

th5.evidence: Integrated refining, chemical plants and Exxon, Mobil and Esso marketing networks give it reliable outlets for its products.

durable.evidence: Low-cost resources should keep it among the leaders for decades, but oil demand may decline over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: It saw Guyana's potential early and holds 45% of the Stabroek block, a unique resource, but the opportunity is now well understood.

trend.evidence: ExxonMobil is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud; rising power demand helps gas but the energy transition is a headwind.

dr1.evidence: TTM EPS rose to $7.76 from $6.70 in 2025 and 2026 consensus revenue of about $415.5B is up about 28% on the oil spike.

dr2.evidence: Guyana and Permian volumes and cost savings should help, but oil prices may fall from 2026 levels.

dr4.evidence: Supply disruption favours it now, but a slowing economy or a Hormuz resolution could push oil back toward $70-75.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include the fifth Guyana FPSO in 4Q26, Golden Pass LNG and Permian growth of about 200,000 barrels a day in 2026.

dr7.evidence: It could be a large position for an oil-bull macro view, but dependence on commodity prices limits conviction.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 30% and operating margin about 11%, typical of a commodity business without pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Free-cash-flow yield is about 4.3% ($30.6B TTM FCF), reasonable but flattered by high oil prices.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 18.6, an operating earnings yield of about 5.4%.

pa2.evidence: The industry is in an upswing driven by the 2026 oil-price spike, not a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: Low debt and low-cost barrels limit permanent loss for the company, but buying near record highs after an oil spike carries real price risk.

wo1.evidence: ExxonMobil is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics, though it is developing lithium and battery graphite.

wo2.evidence: Oil and gas production costs are not falling fast enough to open large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several ARK-style innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Earnings depend heavily on oil, gas and chemical prices.

ns1.evidence: As a price taker, it keeps scale savings as margin rather than sharing them to widen a moat.

ns4.evidence: Guyana and the Permian strengthen its cost position, but long-term oil demand makes a clearly stronger position in 10-20 years uncertain.

va2.evidence: It supplies fuels, gas and plastics that billions of people need for transport, heating, power and everyday goods.

tn1.evidence: ExxonMobil is a century-old oil, gas and chemicals producer; rising power demand helps gas and it is developing lithium and carbon capture, but it is not built for a secular trend like AI or the energy transition.

tn2.evidence: The market sees ExxonMobil as an integrated oil major, and that is what it is; there is no gap between story and reality.

tn3.evidence: ExxonMobil is a commodity producer whose earnings follow oil and gas prices, one of the zones Nash avoids.

tn4.evidence: It passes only one of three: it is profitable ($28,844M in 2025), but revenue fell in 2023 and 2025 ($339,247M to $323,905M) and debt of $42,368M exceeded cash of $10,588M at June 30, 2026.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each of the six quarters to June 2026 ($2,235M to $17,028M), but debt exceeded cash in every one, for example $42,368M vs $10,588M at June 30, 2026.

tn6.evidence: Revenue rose 44.1% in Q2 2026 and 23.1% in the first half on the oil-price spike, but trailing twelve-month growth is about 9.6% and FY2025 revenue fell 4.5%.

tn7.evidence: First-half revenue growth of 23.1% plus a trailing free-cash-flow margin of 8.5% ($30,553M on $361,060M) gives about 32, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In the first half of 2026 revenue rose 23.1% ($197,690M vs $160,535M) while costs before operating income rose 22.7%, lifting operating income to $23,448M from $18,554M.

tn9.evidence: It fails two instant kills: debt exceeds cash ($42,368M vs $10,588M) and the trailing operating margin is 11.2%, below 20%, though short interest is only 0.97%.

tn10.evidence: There is no existential threat, but ExxonMobil faces climate-deception lawsuits from US states and cities and methane and carbon rules.

tn11.evidence: ExxonMobil provides crude oil, natural gas, fuels and chemicals that help drivers, airlines and manufacturers power vehicles and make products, and charges market prices per barrel, cubic foot or tonne; customers choose it for reliable supply and integration, not differentiation.

tn13.evidence: Total 65 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0 (about 9.6% trailing), operating margin 5 (11.2%), short interest 10 (0.97%), institutional ownership 10 (66.7%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return 10 (27.9% a year vs SPY's 13.2%, StockAnalysis), moat 5, CEO 5, recession-proof pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2023 and 2025, operating margin dropped from 17.1% (2022) to 10.9% (2025), free cash flow fell from $58,390M (2022) to $23,612M (2025) and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 52x, assets of $464,482M are 2.34x liabilities of $198,371M (goodwill is not material), the current ratio is 1.13 and liabilities are 0.75x equity (June 30, 2026).

tn18.evidence: Darren Woods has delivered Guyana growth, the Pioneer deal and cost cuts since becoming CEO in January 2017, but he is not a founder, is just short of 10 years in the role and no open-market purchases by him were found.

tn20.evidence: ExxonMobil beat EPS estimates in Q3 2025, Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 but missed in Q2 2026 ($3.52 adjusted vs $3.56 expected), per OpenCapital.

tn21.evidence: It has a single CEO, no accounting concerns or auditor change, and its 2023-24 Denbury and Pioneer deals were strategic rather than a spree; insider sales were small (about $2.4M in a year).

tn22.evidence: ExxonMobil has $361B of trailing revenue, strong profits and buys back shares, so it is not a hype trap.

tn24.evidence: Holding the trailing 8.5% FCF margin, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth, the $174.08 price implies about 20% annual revenue growth for five years, far above the 3-year average of -6.4% and trailing growth of about 9.6%.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year average revenue growth of -6.4%, an 8.8% average FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and $31,780M of net debt, value is about $56 per share, far below $174.08.

tn26.evidence: The forward P/E of 13.3 is in line with oil-major peers, but the PEG ratio is 1.36 (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), above Nash's limit of 1.
